definition: General Data Protection Regulation — EU law that controls how organisations collect, store and use personal data. Gives individuals rights over their data including access and erasure.
Software as a Service — cloud-delivered software accessed via a browser. The provider hosts and maintains the software. Examples: Google Docs, Office 365, Salesforce.
Infrastructure as a Service — cloud-provided computing resources such as virtual machines, storage and networking. Example: Amazon AWS, Microsoft Azure.
Platform as a Service — cloud environment providing tools to develop, test and deploy applications without managing underlying infrastructure. Example: Google App Engine.
A social engineering attack using fraudulent emails or websites to trick users into revealing passwords, financial details or personal information.
Malicious software designed to disrupt, damage or gain unauthorised access to systems. Includes viruses, worms, trojans, spyware and ransomware.
A type of malware that encrypts the victim's files and demands a ransom payment (usually cryptocurrency) in exchange for the decryption key.
A network security device or software that monitors and filters incoming/outgoing traffic based on predefined rules to block unauthorised access.
The process of converting readable data (plaintext) into an unreadable format (ciphertext) using an algorithm, so only authorised parties with the key can read it.
A security process requiring two or more verification factors to access a system — e.g. password + SMS code + biometric scan.
A backup strategy: keep 3 copies of data, on 2 different media types, with 1 copy stored offsite. Protects against hardware failure, fire and local disasters.
GDPR principle requiring organisations to only collect and process personal data that is strictly necessary for the stated purpose. Reduces privacy risk.
GDPR right (also called 'right to be forgotten') allowing individuals to request that an organisation deletes their personal data under certain circumstances.
The maximum rate of data transfer across a network connection, measured in bits per second (Mbps/Gbps). Higher bandwidth allows more simultaneous data transfer.
Delivery of computing services — servers, storage, databases, software — over the internet ('the cloud'), allowing on-demand access and scalable resources.
Central Processing Unit — the 'brain' of a computer that fetches, decodes and executes instructions. Contains ALU, control unit and registers. Speed measured in GHz.
Random Access Memory — volatile, fast, temporary storage that holds data and instructions currently in use. Lost when power is cut. Measured in GB.
Read Only Memory — non-volatile memory that retains contents when powered off. Stores firmware/BIOS needed to start the computer. Cannot be easily modified.
Very small, extremely fast memory located on or near the CPU. Stores frequently used instructions/data to reduce CPU waiting time. Has L1, L2, L3 levels.
Arithmetic Logic Unit — component of the CPU that performs arithmetic operations (add, subtract) and logical comparisons (AND, OR, NOT).
Solid State Drive — storage using flash memory chips with no moving parts. Faster read/write speeds, more reliable, uses less power, but more expensive per GB than HDD.
Hard Disk Drive — storage using spinning magnetic platters and read/write heads. Lower cost per GB, higher capacity, but slower, heavier and more prone to mechanical failure.
A technique where the OS uses hard disk space as an overflow for RAM when physical RAM is full. Much slower than RAM but allows larger programs to run.
Network Interface Card — hardware component that connects a computer to a network. Can be wired (Ethernet) or wireless (Wi-Fi). Has a unique MAC address.
Network device that connects multiple networks together and directs data packets between them using IP addresses. Also assigns local IP addresses via DHCP.
Software owned and controlled by a company. Source code is closed. Users must pay for licences and cannot modify the software. Example: Microsoft Windows.
Software with publicly available source code that anyone can view, modify and distribute. Often free. Example: Linux, LibreOffice, Firefox.
System software that manages hardware resources, provides a user interface and enables applications to run. Examples: Windows 11, macOS, Linux, Android.
Programs that perform maintenance and optimisation tasks on a computer. Examples: antivirus, disk defragmenter, backup software, file compression tools.
Graphics Processing Unit — specialised processor designed to handle graphics rendering and parallel processing tasks. Used in gaming, video editing and AI computing.
A named storage location in memory that holds a value which can change during program execution. Must be declared with a name and usually a data type.
A named value that is set once and cannot change during program execution. Used for fixed values like PI = 3.14159. Improves code readability and maintainability.
A whole number data type with no decimal point. Can be positive, negative or zero. Examples: -10, 0, 5, 1000. Used for counting and index values.
A data type with only two possible values: True or False. Used in conditions and logical expressions. Named after mathematician George Boole.
A data type representing a sequence of characters (text). Stored in quotes. Examples: "Hello", "RA10". Operations include concatenation, length and substring.
A programming construct that repeats a block of code. FOR loops repeat a fixed number of times; WHILE loops repeat while a condition is true.
A programming construct that chooses between different paths of execution based on a condition. Implemented using IF / ELSE IF / ELSE statements.
The most basic control structure — instructions are executed one after another in the order they are written, from top to bottom.
A named, reusable block of code that performs a specific task. Can accept parameters as inputs and return a value. Reduces repetition and improves code organisation.
A variable defined in a function's signature that receives a value (argument) when the function is called. Allows functions to work with different input data.
A precise, step-by-step set of instructions designed to solve a specific problem or perform a task. Can be expressed as pseudocode, flowchart or code.
An informal, plain-English description of an algorithm that uses programming-like structure without strict syntax rules. Used to plan code before writing it.
An error caused by breaking the grammar rules of a programming language, e.g. missing brackets or misspelling a keyword. Prevents the program from running.
An error where the program runs without crashing but produces the wrong output due to a mistake in the algorithm or conditions. Hardest type to find.
A method of manually tracing code execution by recording variable values at each step. Used to find logic errors and verify algorithm correctness.
